standard.title: Collect, organise and represent geographical data
standard.description: collect, organise and represent data and information from primary research methods, including fieldwork and secondary research materials, using geospatial technologies and digital tools as appropriate
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have prior data collection and organisation skills from F–6 HASS (AC9HS6S02: locate, collect and organise information and data from primary and secondary sources in a range of formats). This standard introduces geospatial technologies, specialist digital tools, cartographic conventions and the distinction between primary fieldwork methods and secondary research materials in a specifically geographical context.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students collect, organise and represent geographical data from primary and secondary sources using appropriate geospatial technologies, digital tools and cartographic conventions.

nodes.label: Primary fieldwork methods for geographical data
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify appropriate primary research methods for a geographical inquiry, including fieldwork, and use specialised digital tools to collect original materials.
nodes.minimum_width: Students identify at least two primary fieldwork methods appropriate to a geographical inquiry and explain what kind of data each produces.
nodes.typical_width: Students identify appropriate primary research methods including interview and survey data, photographs of streetscapes, annotated field sketches, diagrams and statistics related to liveability or water — and use specialised digital tools (e.g. survey platforms, mapping apps) to collect original materials from a field context.
wider: Conduct fieldwork using at least two different primary methods (e.g. survey + field sketch + photographs) and reflect on what each method captures and what it misses
Design a fieldwork data collection protocol including the questions, observation prompts and recording formats needed — evaluate the protocol before going to the field
Compare fieldwork data collected using different methods for the same site and identify agreements and discrepancies
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot select appropriate primary methods and tools for a geographical inquiry will produce data that does not match the inquiry question. The mismatch between question, method and data undermines the entire inquiry cycle — analysis and conclusion cannot proceed meaningfully from poorly matched data.

response_modes.reason: Selecting a primary method requires reasoning about what data type the question needs and which method produces that type. Scaffolding: inquiry question → data type needed → method that produces that data type → tool for that method. This chain prevents method selection by familiarity rather than fitness.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two primary research methods appropriate to a specific geographical inquiry question and explains what data each produces.
Uses at least one digital tool to support primary data collection and explains why it was selected.

nodes.label: Secondary research: finding and selecting relevant materials
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can collect relevant secondary research materials using advanced search functions, evaluating relevance and reliability.
nodes.minimum_width: Students locate at least two relevant secondary sources for a geographical inquiry and explain why each is relevant.
nodes.typical_width: Students collect relevant secondary research materials — print and online publications, photographs, images, statistical datasets — using advanced search functions (e.g. specific field search operators) and explain the criteria used to assess relevance and reliability.
wider: Compare two secondary sources on the same topic (e.g. two reports on water scarcity in a region) and evaluate their reliability, currency and perspective

Examine the difference between primary and secondary use of the same material — e.g. an aerial photograph used as primary evidence of current land use vs used as secondary evidence from a historical archive
Practise advanced search operators to narrow results to relevant sources and evaluate whether the results are genuinely more useful

response_modes.reason: Reliable source selection requires repeated practice with explicit criteria. Students need multiple search exercises with structured reflection on what was found and why it was or was not suitable.

success_criteria: Locates at least two secondary sources relevant to a geographical inquiry question and explains the criteria used to assess each source's relevance.
Uses at least one advanced search method to find sources and reflects on how it improved search results.

nodes.label: Representing data in appropriate geographical formats
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can represent geographical data and information in formats appropriate to the data type and inquiry question — including tables, graphs, and geospatial representations.
nodes.minimum_width: Students represent collected data in at least one appropriate format and explain why that format was chosen.
nodes.typical_width: Students represent data in appropriate formats — combining primary research data into questionnaires, tables or graphs; representing spatial information using cartographic conventions in maps at different scales using computer mapping tools.
wider: Represent the same dataset in two different formats (e.g. table and choropleth map) and evaluate which better communicates the spatial pattern
Construct a map conforming to full cartographic conventions (title, scale, north arrow, legend, projection note) for a geographical distribution and evaluate its accuracy and readability
Use geospatial software (e.g. Google My Maps, ArcGIS Online) to represent spatial data and reflect on how digital tools alter what can be represented and communicated
nodes.hinge_reason: Data representation is the bridge between collection and analysis. Students who cannot represent data in geographically appropriate formats — particularly spatial representation with cartographic conventions — cannot engage with S03 pattern and trend analysis. A table where a map is needed, or a map without conventions, prevents spatial pattern reading.

response_modes.reason: Cartographic conventions require repeated practice to apply correctly and consistently. Students need practice constructing maps with all required conventions — not just exposure to examples.
Representing both spatial (map) and non-spatial (graph, table) data, and comparing which format serves which question, builds genuine understanding of representation as a communication choice.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Format selection as a deliberate communication choice — not just a technical requirement — is a sophisticated data literacy skill. Students who can argue for their format choice based on what the data type demands are developing transferable analytical reasoning.
success_criteria: Represents geographical data in at least one format (map, table, graph) that is appropriate to the data type and inquiry question.
Applies cartographic conventions (title, scale, north arrow, legend) to any map produced.

nodes.label: Integration: collect, organise and represent in an inquiry context
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students collect, organise and represent data from primary and secondary sources using appropriate geospatial and digital tools — producing a coherent evidence base for a geographical inquiry.
nodes.minimum_width: Students produce a small evidence base (at least one primary and one secondary source) organised and represented in appropriate formats for a specific inquiry question.
nodes.typical_width: Students produce an evidence base for a geographical inquiry that combines primary and secondary data, organises it into appropriate formats, uses geospatial technologies where applicable, and presents it in forms that support analysis of the inquiry question.
wider: Develop a full evidence base for a geographical inquiry using at least three different data sources and two different representation formats — evaluate which combinations produce the most useful analytical base
Reflect on the quality of the evidence base produced: which inquiry questions are well-supported and which have evidence gaps? What would strengthen the base?

response_modes.reason: The integration node connects the three earlier nodes — method selection, source finding, representation — into a coherent evidence base for a specific inquiry. The performance is the production of evidence fit for purpose, not the demonstration of each skill in isolation.

success_criteria: Produces an evidence base using at least one primary and one secondary source, represented in appropriate formats for the inquiry question.
Reflects on one limitation or gap in the evidence base and explains what additional evidence would address it.
